research.lead: Two labs so far, both asking a version of the same question: can you trust what the instrument just told you, and can anyone reproduce it tomorrow?

positions.name: Mass cytometry at the Vaccine & Immunotherapy Center
bullets: Replaced hand-called immune populations with a reproducible Python pipeline, running across vaccine stimulations on datasets past a million events.
Cut raw instrument output to usable populations in one pass — FCS parsing, arcsinh transformation and dimensionality reduction in a single path instead of three manual steps.
Made cluster assignments hold up to immunological review rather than just look clean, by adding biological validation metrics to the existing clustering.
Extended the pipeline to new cohorts, using X-shift to find where population abundance has moved and carrying across the Shannon and Simpson diversity notebooks I wrote for the first project.

projects.title: Projects — Ben Silver
projects.description: CraveCast, a craving forecaster for addiction recovery, and EpiAlert, allergen detection and epinephrine mapping for travellers.
projects.heading: Projects
projects.lead: Both of these started with a problem someone I know actually had. Neither of them is a demo.

items.name: CraveCast
paragraphs: CraveCast warns people in recovery before a craving lands, instead of recording it afterwards. The forecast comes from their own logs and the peer-reviewed ADARP study.

Underneath it is kernel density estimation over the hours someone has actually logged a craving, read against the study's population-level risk windows — useful on the first day, personal by the second week. It runs entirely in the browser and works offline, so nothing about a person's recovery leaves their device. Getting a published model to actually run taught me the parts that aren't in the paper: choosing a bandwidth, deciding what counts as a signal, and working out how you'd know whether a prediction was any good.

The idea came from a lung transplant observership at Mass General. COPD is one of the most common reasons people end up needing new lungs, and smoking is the leading cause of COPD. I wanted to build something for the addiction end of that, not the surgical end.

It also had to be worth opening. Recovery apps tend to be either a logbook or a clinical dashboard, and neither is what you reach for in the moment you need it. This one has streaks, unlocks and some colour — breaking an addiction is hard enough without the tool being another chore.

facts.label: Built with
facts.value: HTML, JavaScript, Python, kernel density estimation

items.name: EpiAlert
paragraphs: EpiAlert turns a photo of a meal into an allergen decision in seconds, with the nearest stocked epinephrine on the same screen.

I grew up in Taiwan with a nut allergy. I know now that pad thai usually has crushed peanuts in it and that a lot of Indian curries are thickened with cashews. A shy nine-year-old doesn't, and isn't going to ask a waiter. This is the check I didn't have.

It's a first check, not a verdict, and the app says so. It's built for the unfamiliar meal in a country where you can't be sure the waiter understood the question — enough to settle it, or to tell you this is one to ask about properly. It remembers your allergies, and it's simple enough for a kid to use at the table.
I cut a peer-review feed late in development. Crowd-sourced safety data is a liability when the failure mode is anaphylaxis.

facts.label: Built with
facts.value: Python, Flask, Claude Vision API, Google Maps API

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Repository private, happy to walk through it

about.title: About — Ben Silver
about.description: Computer science and biology at Tufts, research computing at Tufts Technology Services, and where Ben Silver would like this to go next.
about.heading: About
paragraphs: I came to Tufts for computer science and added a focus in biological sciences once it turned out biology was the part I couldn't stop reading about. The two looked unrelated for about a year, and then stopped being unrelated at all.

I grew up in a Taiwanese-American household, where the answer to most questions was to take the lid off and look. That's more or less the whole story. A bike that shifts badly gets stripped to the frame; a knife that won't bite gets a whetstone and an argument about angles; a dataset with a million immune cells in it gets a pipeline until the clusters mean something.

At Tufts Technology Services I build tooling for research storage. The old request workflow had staff retyping the same details into a fixed format by hand — mine takes a paste, picks the template for the kind of request, and formats it. That's about a quarter of the time back on each one, one consistent format at the end, and nothing for a new starter to memorise.

Data is one big haystack and computer science is the magnet. Finding the pattern and getting it in front of someone who can act on it is most of why I like this work. Biotech and healthcare data are where I'd most like it to land, though prediction, patterns and making numbers usable travel anywhere data does.

second.name: Bikes, mostly in pieces
second.blurb: I ride mountain bikes, and the half I like best is the one where the bike is on the floor in pieces. Brakes bled and upgraded, a dropper post fitted, headset and gears dialled in, a new cassette — most of what's on mine now, I put there. Down to cable ends that match the frame, which nobody notices but me.
